extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; poets and critics interested in religious sentiment and poetic form
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and critical observations about religious poetry and religious sentiment in lyric/dramatic poems, contrasting pagan popular hymns (Theocritus) with medieval Christian popular poetry (St. Francis) and discussing what makes such poetry elevating, consoling, popular, or excessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide-embracing abundance (quantity over quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work 'embraces the whole range of human interests; ... like one of the great Middle-Age Cathedrals, it is in itself a study for a life.' "Quantity rather than quality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value can lie in breadth, variety, infinite suggestiveness and abundance rather than in 'splendour of form' or faultless editing. Expect common paper, ugly type, indifferent editing and misprints; appreciate the collection for range and stimulus rather than editorial perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of impartiality / the necessity of reader's criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do not seek in it impartiality, the critical spirit; in reading it you must do the criticism for yourself; it loves criticism as little as the world loves it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize editorial or collective works may be partisan: they 'put forward all the pros for its own notion, suppress all the contras.' The reader/critic must supply balance and independent judgement rather than expect neutrality from the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative poem = popular use / mass-listenability
rubrics_metrics.description: "To be a representative poem, it must be one for popular use, one that the multitude listens to."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a piece represents a religious sentiment broadly, assess its uptake by and suitability for the multitude — simplicity, repeated performance, and social embedding are key indicators of representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom, animation, gaiety, naturalness, masterly form
rubrics_metrics.description: On Theocritus's idyll: 'a page torn fresh out of the book of human life. What freedom! What animation! What gaiety! What naturalness!... the form is still Theocritus's own, and how excellent is that form, how masterly!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praises characteristics to look for in dramatic/popular poetry: immediacy, liveliness, natural dialogue and a distinctive, masterful formal shape even when borrowing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious emotion and consoling character (absent vs present)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of religious emotion, in our acceptation of the words, and of the comfort springing from religious emotion, not a particle" (speaking of the Greek hymn to Adonis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a text supplies 'religious emotion' as understood in the critic's sense — i.e., elevating, consoling strains (e.g., Kyrie eleison, Te Deum) — rather than mere ritual or festive formalities. Absence of consoling religious affect weakens its claim as 'religious' in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic treatment enabling elevation and consolation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Symbolically treated ... this story was capable of a noble and touching application, and could lead the soul to elevating and consoling thoughts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should note whether myth/ritual material is handled symbolically (transfigured) rather than merely sensually: symbolism allows a poem to point beyond literal pleasure to spiritual consolation and moral elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match of tone to audience; seriousness vs light-heartedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek hymn 'adapts itself exactly to the tone and temper of a gay and pleasure-loving multitude... people who seem never made to be serious, never made to be sick or sorry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the tone suits intended popular audience; a work tailored to light-hearted, pleasure-loving listeners may succeed as popular poetry yet lack seriousness or consolatory depth. Matching tone is a virtue for popular function but may be a limitation for religious profundity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit religion/poetry for popular use; accessibility (language, form)
rubrics_metrics.description: On St. Francis: 'He made poetry. Latin was too learned for this simple, popular nature, and he composed in his mother tongue, in Italian... artless in language, irregular in rhythm, it matches with the childlike genius that produced it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility — vernacular language, artless diction, irregular but natural rhythm — is a positive criterion when the aim is to 'fit religion for popular use.' Formal simplicity that matches popular capacities is a mark of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of whole human experience transfigured by spiritual emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The second admits the whole world, rough and smooth, painful and pleasure-giving, all alike, but all transfigured by the power of a spiritual emotion ... It can thus even say: 'Praised be my Lord for our sister, the death of the body.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A religious poem of depth acknowledges pain, mortality and hardship alongside joy, and transfigures them via spiritual feeling. Inclusion of suffering (not suppression) and its integration into praise/meaning is a criterion of profundity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide refuge and consolation for mass misery
rubrics_metrics.description: "Man should take refuge in his heart and imagination from his misery... one understands the charm for them of a refuge" (especially for the vast majority and in Middle Ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether poetry/religion offers imaginative/heart-felt refuge and consolation to ordinary people living difficult lives; social context (widespread poverty, suffering) makes this function crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of extremes; preference for balance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Human nature is neither all senses and understanding, nor all heart and imagination... Humanity, in its violent rebound from one extreme, had swung from Pompeii to Monte Alverno; but it was sure not to stay there."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique works that push human sentiment to extremes (pure sensualism or ascetic spiritualism). A balanced representation of human nature is implied as healthier and more sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical humility: 'let humanity decide'
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great art of criticism is to get oneself out of the way and to let humanity decide."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a method: critics should avoid imposing personal authority or absolute verdicts; rather, observe how works are received and function socially and historically, allowing general human response to be a guiding measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability test: performance under sickness/adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Can a man live by it? does it help, does it console? ... Heine, stricken with incurable disease... shows the religion of pleasure fails under real sickness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a sentiment/poem by whether it sustains and consoles under real suffering and adversity; popularity or aesthetic charm in prosperity is insufficient if the work offers no solace in illness, grief, or exile.
